items.text: F-rank porter Kang Do-yoon dies in the Seoul Collapse ten years from now and wakes on the morning of his awakening measurement at twenty-seven. He knows the Collapse's mastermind, "the Watcher", is Hunter Association Chairman Yoon Jae-kyung—and he cannot prove it. He builds power quietly to stop the Collapse, but the future starts to slip every time he intervenes.
Primary genre hunter-gate with a regression overlay; English manuscript in the Korean serialized-webnovel tradition.
Violence within a 15+ rating; no sexual content.
Target 180 chapters of about 2,500 words each.
Chapter 1 opens on the measurement device showing F.
Do-yoon tells no one about the regression before ch.58.
Park Mu-jin does not die in Season 1.
The Watcher's identity is not revealed before ch.120.
Romance is slow-burn: no confession and no physical intimacy before ch.87.
Cold, tense tone with intermittent humor; fast pace.
Short sentences; exposition through action and dialogue; hindsight monologue at most 20% of a chapter.
Occasional forum interludes as a device.
Awakened ranks run F through S and are read from measurement devices; there are no status windows.
Mana stones are the currency of the hunter economy.

explanations.rationale: The intake says 'no status windows—only measurement-device readings' and an F–S scale, so the world rule is stated explicitly rather than left implicit.
The intake mentions a 'mana-stone economy' without defining it; treating mana stones as the hunter currency is the minimal reading.

json.text:
The measurement device screamed.

[F]

Red letters. The same red letters as ten years ago.

“F-rank. Porter registration is the window on your left.”

The officer was already calling the next name. Jung Min-jae, according to the badge. He did not look up. He never had.

Do-yoon looked down at his palm. It wasn’t shaking. There was no reason for it to shake. In this whole room, he was the only one who knew how far this hand could go.

*March twelfth.*

Gangnam. Three things to finish before then.

Behind him someone laughed, the short bark of a man who had just read a B on the panel and wanted the room to know it. Ten years ago Do-yoon had turned around to look. This time he didn’t. He knew the man’s name, knew the guild that would sign him, knew the gate that would swallow him in year four.

None of that was his problem today.

“Next. Kang Do-yoon, step away from the device.”

“Yes, sir.”

He stepped away. The panel went dark behind him, and a nineteen-year-old with dyed hair took his place and held her breath the way everyone did.

Do-yoon walked toward the window on the left. His legs remembered the route better than his head did; he had walked it once before, on the worst morning of a life that had ended badly.

The morning was the same. The building was the same. The letter on the panel was the same.

He was not.

json.text:
The porter registration window had a line of three. All of them F-rank. All of them avoiding each other’s eyes.

“Name.”

“Kang Do-yoon.”

“Age.”

“Twenty-seven.”

The clerk typed, stamped, slid a laminated card across the counter without looking at it. PORTER — CLASS F. Association Registry No. 88-0412. Do-yoon knew the number before he read it.

“You’ll want a party,” the clerk said. “Porters who go in alone don’t come out.”

“I know.”

“Board’s on the wall. Good luck.”

The board was a corkboard. Paper slips, phone numbers, the occasional photo. Ten years ago he had stood in front of it for forty minutes and picked wrong.

He didn’t look at the board. He looked at the bench beside it.

Park Mu-jin sat with his arms crossed and his boots planted like he was daring the floor to move. Forty-five, C-rank, a jaw that had been broken once and set badly. He was reading a folded newspaper and not reading it at all.

Do-yoon’s throat closed for exactly one second. Then he made it open.

“Mister Park.”

Mu-jin looked up. “Do I know you, kid?”

“No, sir. The Association posted that you’re looking for a porter. D-gate, Mapo, tomorrow.”

“I posted that an hour ago.” Mu-jin folded the paper. “You read fast for an F.”

“I carry fast, too.”

The older man looked at him for a long moment—at the card in his hand, the letter on it, the hands that were not shaking.

“Pay is eight percent of the stones. You carry what I tell you and you run when I tell you.”

“Yes, sir.”

“Six a.m. Don’t be late.” Mu-jin stood, and he was shorter than Do-yoon remembered. “What did you say your name was?”

“Kang Do-yoon.”

“Mister Park,” Mu-jin repeated, tasting it, and snorted. “Nobody’s called me that in twenty years. Fine. Kid.”

Park Mu-jin takes Do-yoon on as porter for the Mapo D-gate run at 6 a.m. tomorrow, eight percent of the stones.

json.text:
Outside, the Mapo sky was the color of a wet sidewalk.

Do-yoon stood on the steps of the measurement hall and let the cold get into his jacket. It was exactly same feeling with ten years ago. That was the point. He needed to feel it and not flinch.

He took out his phone. The date on the lock screen was the date he expected. Day zero.

He opened a blank note and typed three lines.

*1. The gate run. Do not let him take the left corridor.*

*2. The compass.*

*3. The Chairman.*

He stared at the third line for a while. Then he deleted it. Some things were safer as memory than as text, even on a phone nobody would ever search.

Two lines. That was enough to start with.

A bus hissed past. A girl on the steps below him was crying into her sleeve, an F-card crushed in her fist. Ten years ago he had done the same thing, three steps to the left. He had cried for an hour and then gone home and not come back for two weeks.

He walked down past her. He did not say anything. There was nothing anyone could have said to him, either.

At the bottom of the steps his phone buzzed.

Park Mu-jin: Tomorrow. 6 a.m. Gate 3, Mapo. Don’t be late, kid.

Do-yoon read it twice.

Last time, Mu-jin had sent the same message. The same words, the same time. Last time, Do-yoon had been late, and Mu-jin had gone in without a porter, and had come out on a stretcher with the left leg of his trousers cut away.

He typed back one word.

*Understood.*

Then he put the phone in his pocket and started walking toward the station, toward a room he had not seen in ten years, toward a morning he was going to spend making sure an old man did not die for him a second time.

The first thing on the list was tomorrow.
